name: Majid Al Futtaim Properties
desc: Develops and operates shopping malls such as Mall of the Emirates and City Centre, plus hotels and residential communities.
markets: Malls, hotels and communities in the UAE and other Middle East and North Africa markets such as Oman, Bahrain and Egypt.
rationale: High-footfall Gulf malls and hotels suit fan activations, retail promotions and hospitality around the Abu Dhabi and other Gulf Grands Prix.

name: Cushman & Wakefield
desc: Commercial real estate services firm providing leasing, capital markets, valuation and property and facility management to occupiers and investors.
markets: Offices in nearly 60 countries across the Americas, Europe, Middle East and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Global B2B firm whose corporate occupier and investor clients could be hosted through F1 hospitality across many race markets.

name: Mohawk Industries
desc: Manufactures carpet, ceramic tile, laminate, vinyl and wood flooring under brands including Mohawk, Daltile, Unilin and Quick-Step.
markets: Main markets North America and Europe, with operations in Latin America and Australia and New Zealand.
rationale: Flooring maker with consumer brands in the US and Europe; F1 could support trade and retailer hospitality, but the fit is indirect.

name: Vingroup
desc: Vietnamese conglomerate active in real estate, retail property, hotels, healthcare, education and electric vehicles through VinFast.
markets: Mainly Vietnam; VinFast sells electric vehicles in North America, Europe and several Asian markets.
rationale: VinFast's push into the US, Europe and Asia needs global brand awareness; F1 could showcase the group's mobility and technology ambitions.

name: City Developments Limited
desc: Develops and owns residential, office and retail property and owns hotels through Millennium & Copthorne in many countries.
markets: Singapore core market, with property and hotels in the UK, US, Japan, China, Australia and other countries.
rationale: Singapore Grand Prix host-city developer with international hotels; F1 hospitality could support premium residential sales and hotel marketing.

name: Somnigroup International
desc: Makes Tempur-Pedic, Sealy and Stearns & Foster mattresses and runs Mattress Firm retail stores, selling to consumers and retailers.
markets: Largest market the United States; Tempur and Sealy products are sold across Europe, Asia-Pacific and other international markets.
rationale: Consumer mattress brands that use sports marketing; F1 could promote sleep and recovery performance messages internationally.
changed: Renamed from Tempur Sealy International after acquiring Mattress Firm in 2025

name: Kalyan Jewellers
desc: Retails gold, diamond and gemstone jewellery through showrooms and the Candere online brand, mainly for weddings and festivals.
markets: Showrooms across India, the Middle East and the United States; India is the main market.
rationale: Strong consumer brand expanding in the Gulf and US; F1 could reach affluent Indian and Gulf audiences, though fit is moderate.

name: Coty
desc: Makes and sells fragrances, cosmetics and skincare under owned and licensed brands such as CoverGirl, Rimmel, Burberry and Hugo Boss.
markets: Sells across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the Middle East through retailers and online.
rationale: Global prestige fragrance portfolio suits glamorous F1 launches and travel-retail activations in key race markets.

name: The Estée Lauder Companies
desc: Makes and sells prestige skincare, makeup, fragrance and haircare under brands such as Estée Lauder, Clinique, MAC and La Mer.
markets: Sells in about 150 countries, with large businesses in the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific and travel retail.
rationale: Prestige beauty portfolio with global reach; F1's growing female audience and luxury hospitality fit product launches and travel retail.

name: Shein
desc: Online fast-fashion retailer selling low-cost clothing, beauty, home goods and accessories directly to consumers through its app and website.
markets: Sells to consumers in over 150 countries, mainly Europe, the Americas, the Middle East and Australia.
rationale: Huge young consumer audience overlaps with F1's new fans, but labour and environmental scrutiny raise brand-safety questions.

name: e.l.f. Beauty
desc: Sells affordable cosmetics and skincare under e.l.f. Cosmetics, e.l.f. SKIN, Naturium and rhode through mass retailers and online.
markets: Mainly United States, with sales in Canada, the UK, Europe and other international markets.
rationale: Social-media-driven beauty brand targeting Gen Z; F1's young female audience growth offers a fit for international expansion.
changed: Acquired rhode in 2025

name: Moncler
desc: Luxury fashion house selling down jackets, outerwear and ready-to-wear under Moncler and Stone Island through boutiques and online.
markets: Sells worldwide through own stores and wholesale, with large businesses in Asia, Europe and the Americas.
rationale: Global luxury brand; F1 paddock audiences and lifestyle events suit high-end apparel collaborations and VIP hospitality.
changed: Acquired Stone Island in 2021

name: Frasers Group
desc: Retail group owning Sports Direct, House of Fraser, Flannels, Evans Cycles and GAME, selling to consumers in stores and online.
markets: Mainly the UK and Ireland, with Sports Direct stores across continental Europe.
rationale: Mass-market sports retailer; F1 merchandise and fan activations could drive traffic in UK and European stores.

name: Tapestry
desc: Fashion holding company selling Coach and Kate Spade New York handbags, accessories and footwear through stores, wholesale and online.
markets: Sells in North America, Greater China, Japan, Europe and other Asian markets.
rationale: Coach's global luxury positioning could use F1 lifestyle and young-fan reach, especially in the US and China.
changed: Sold Stuart Weitzman to Caleres in 2025

name: Birkenstock
desc: Makes and sells sandals, clogs and shoes with contoured cork footbeds through wholesale, own stores and e-commerce.
markets: Sells in over 100 countries, with main markets in the Americas and Europe and growing Asia-Pacific sales.
rationale: Global lifestyle footwear brand; F1 collaborations could reach young fans, though comfort sandals have limited motorsport tie-in.
changed: Listed on the NYSE in 2023

name: JD Sports Fashion
desc: Retails sports footwear and apparel from brands such as Nike and adidas through JD, Finish Line and other store chains.
markets: Operates mainly in Europe, North America and Asia-Pacific through thousands of stores and online.
rationale: Youth sports-fashion retailer active in sponsorship; F1 merchandise and young-fan reach fit its US and European growth.
changed: Acquired Hibbett in 2024

name: Golden Goose
desc: Italian luxury fashion company selling handcrafted distressed sneakers, apparel and accessories through boutiques, department stores and online.
markets: Sells through boutiques and partners in Europe, North America and Asia.
rationale: Luxury sneaker brand popular with affluent young buyers; F1 lifestyle collaborations and paddock visibility could fit.

name: Ralph Lauren
desc: Designs and sells apparel, footwear, accessories, fragrance and home goods under Polo Ralph Lauren, Lauren and other labels.
markets: Sells through own stores, wholesale and online in North America, Europe and Asia.
rationale: Long-time premium sports sponsor (Wimbledon, US Open, golf); F1's luxury hospitality and global audience fit its brand strategy.

name: Under Armour
desc: Designs and sells performance sports apparel, footwear and accessories through wholesale partners, own stores and e-commerce.
markets: Sells in North America, Europe, Middle East and Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
rationale: Performance sportswear brand with heavy sponsorship; team kit or performance apparel deals in F1 would be a natural fit.

name: Gap Inc.
desc: Apparel retailer owning Gap, Old Navy, Banana Republic and Athleta, selling clothing through stores, franchisees and online.
markets: Mainly United States, with company stores in Canada and Japan and franchise stores in many other countries.
rationale: Mass apparel brand focused on the US; F1's growing American audience offers reach, but motorsport fit is limited.

name: Levi Strauss & Co.
desc: Makes and sells denim jeans and apparel under Levi's and Beyond Yoga through wholesale, own stores and online.
markets: Sells in over 100 countries across the Americas, Europe and Asia.
rationale: Iconic global apparel brand with music and sports marketing; F1 merchandise collaborations and fan events could fit.
changed: Sold Dockers to Authentic Brands Group in 2025

name: LPP
desc: Polish fashion group selling clothing and accessories under Reserved, Sinsay, Cropp, House and Mohito in stores and online.
markets: Stores mainly in Central, Eastern and Western Europe, plus franchise stores in the Middle East.
rationale: Fast-growing European fashion retailer; F1 could support Western European expansion, though the motorsport fit is modest.

name: Nike
desc: Designs and sells athletic footwear, apparel and equipment under Nike, Jordan and Converse through retailers and its own channels.
markets: Sells worldwide, with large businesses in North America, Europe, Greater China and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: World's largest sportswear brand; rivals adidas and Puma already sponsor F1 teams, making motorsport a direct competitive arena.

name: Li-Ning
desc: Designs and sells sports footwear, apparel and equipment for running, basketball, badminton and lifestyle mainly in China.
markets: Mainly mainland China, with small international sales through distributors and sponsored athletes.
rationale: Chinese sportswear brand seeking global credibility; F1 and the Chinese Grand Prix could raise its international profile.

name: Kontoor Brands
desc: Apparel company selling Wrangler and Lee denim and Helly Hansen outdoor and workwear through retailers, wholesale and online.
markets: Main market the United States, with sales across Europe, Asia and other international markets.
rationale: Wrangler and Helly Hansen use sports sponsorship; F1 fit is moderate, mainly for Helly Hansen's international technical apparel.
changed: Acquired Helly Hansen in 2025

name: Crocs
desc: Makes and sells Crocs foam clogs, sandals and Jibbitz charms and HEYDUDE casual shoes through retailers and online.
markets: Sells in more than 80 countries across the Americas, Europe and Asia.
rationale: Collaboration-driven consumer brand; F1-themed limited editions could reach young fans globally, though fit is promotional rather than technical.
changed: Acquired HEYDUDE in 2022

name: Anheuser-Busch InBev
desc: World's largest brewer, selling beers including Budweiser, Corona, Stella Artois, Michelob Ultra and Brahma in many countries.
markets: Sells in over 150 countries, with major markets in the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Global beer brands and huge sponsorship budgets; rival Heineken is an F1 global partner, so the category is proven.

name: Thai Beverage
desc: Produces and sells beer, spirits and non-alcoholic drinks, including Chang beer and Sangsom rum, mainly in South-East Asia.
markets: Mainly Thailand and Vietnam, with Scotch whisky distilleries in Scotland and exports to many countries.
rationale: Chang is an established sports sponsor; F1 could build regional Asian brand awareness, while rival Singha already partners F1.

name: Keurig Dr Pepper
desc: Sells soft drinks such as Dr Pepper, Canada Dry and Snapple, plus Keurig coffee brewers and K-Cup pods.
markets: Mainly United States and Canada, with some Mexico sales; JDE Peet's acquisition agreed in 2025 adds global coffee markets.
rationale: Large US beverage marketer; F1's growing US audience suits energy drink GHOST and soft drink promotions, while PepsiCo already partners F1.
changed: Agreed in 2025 to acquire JDE Peet's and announced plans to split into two companies

name: Accor
desc: Hotel group operating and franchising hotels under brands such as Sofitel, Pullman, Novotel, Mercure, ibis, Fairmont and Raffles.
markets: Hotels in over 100 countries across Europe, the Middle East, Asia-Pacific, Africa and the Americas.
rationale: Global hotel brands and ALL loyalty programme could serve F1 travel, race-weekend hospitality and member experiences.

name: Alimentation Couche-Tard
desc: Operates Circle K and Couche-Tard convenience stores and fuel stations, selling fuel, food, drinks and everyday goods.
markets: Company stores in North America and Europe, with licensed Circle K stores in Asia and other regions.
rationale: Circle K fuel and convenience network across North America and Europe suits F1 fan promotions and fuel marketing.
changed: Withdrew its bid for Seven & i Holdings in 2025

name: Danone
desc: Makes dairy and plant-based foods, specialised nutrition and bottled water under brands such as Activia, Alpro, Evian and Aptamil.
markets: Sells in more than 120 markets across Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific and Africa.
rationale: Evian and health-focused brands suit hydration and wellness messaging; F1 could support premium water and nutrition marketing globally.

name: Grab Holdings
desc: Super-app offering ride-hailing, food and grocery delivery, digital payments and financial services to consumers and merchants.
markets: Operates in eight South-East Asian countries, including Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines.
rationale: Dominant South-East Asian consumer platform; Singapore Grand Prix transport, delivery and fan offers make a natural regional fit.
changed: Listed on Nasdaq through a SPAC merger in 2021

name: Diageo
desc: Produces and sells spirits and beer, including Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, Guinness, Tanqueray, Don Julio and Baileys.
markets: Sells in about 180 countries across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Africa and Latin America.
rationale: Former F1 partner through Johnnie Walker; rivals Heineken, Pernod Ricard and William Grant now sponsor F1 and teams.

name: Froneri
desc: Makes and sells ice cream and frozen desserts, including Nestlé-licensed brands, through supermarkets and other retailers.
markets: Operates in Europe, the United States, Australia, Asia and other markets in more than 20 countries.
rationale: Corporate name is little known and consumer brands are largely licensed; F1 value would be limited to brand-level promotions.
changed: Formed in 2016 as a joint venture of Nestlé and PAI Partners

name: The Magnum Ice Cream Company
desc: World's largest ice cream maker, selling Magnum, Wall's, Ben & Jerry's, Cornetto and Breyers through retailers and freezers.
markets: Sells in many countries across Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific and Africa.
rationale: Newly independent company building its global brands; Magnum's premium positioning could suit F1 lifestyle and summer race activations.
changed: Demerged from Unilever and listed in December 2025

name: Yum! Brands
desc: Franchises KFC, Taco Bell, Pizza Hut and Habit Burger & Grill restaurants, earning royalties from franchisees worldwide.
markets: Restaurants in more than 150 countries across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and the Middle East.
rationale: Global fast-food brands with heavy advertising; F1 fan reach in the US, Middle East and Asia could support KFC and Taco Bell.

name: Grupo Nutresa
desc: Produces processed foods including cold cuts, biscuits, chocolates, coffee, ice cream and pasta for consumers and retailers.
markets: Mainly Colombia and other Latin American countries, with operations and sales in the United States.
rationale: Leading Colombian food brands with Latin American reach; F1 fit is limited outside events in Mexico and Brazil.
changed: Control passed to the Gilinski family through a 2024 share swap with Grupo Sura and Grupo Argos

name: Constellation Brands
desc: Brews and imports Mexican beers such as Corona, Modelo and Pacifico for the US market and sells wine and spirits.
markets: Customers mainly in the United States, with breweries in Mexico and wine operations in New Zealand.
rationale: Leading US beer marketer with sports sponsorships; F1's US races in Miami, Austin and Las Vegas fit, though Heineken holds F1's beer rights.
changed: Sold mainstream wine brands to The Wine Group in 2025

name: McCormick & Company
desc: Makes spices, seasonings and condiments such as McCormick, Frank's RedHot and French's, and flavours for food manufacturers.
markets: Sells in about 150 countries, with main markets in the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Pantry brands with limited motorsport link; F1 fit would rely on consumer promotions rather than strategic brand alignment.

name: Mondelez International
desc: Makes snacks and confectionery such as Oreo, Cadbury, Milka, Toblerone and Ritz, sold through retailers worldwide.
markets: Sells in about 150 countries across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and Africa.
rationale: Global snack brands with big marketing budgets; rival Nestlé (KitKat) is an F1 partner, showing the category fits.

name: Subway
desc: Franchises made-to-order sandwich, wrap and salad restaurants, earning royalties and fees from franchisees in over 100 countries.
markets: Restaurants in over 100 countries across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the Middle East.
rationale: Global quick-service brand with heavy advertising; F1 could support international marketing under new private-equity ownership.
changed: Acquired by Roark Capital in 2024

name: Carrefour
desc: Operates hypermarkets, supermarkets, convenience stores and e-commerce, selling groceries and general merchandise directly and through franchisees.
markets: Main markets France, Spain, Belgium, Brazil and Argentina, with franchised stores in the Middle East, Africa and Asia.
rationale: Mass grocery retailer with long sports sponsorship history; F1 promotions could drive traffic, mainly in France, Spain and Brazil.

name: MBRF Global Foods
desc: Produces beef, chicken, pork and processed foods under brands including Sadia, Perdigão and Marfrig for retailers and foodservice.
markets: Brazil core market, with US beef operations, South American plants and exports to more than 100 countries.
rationale: Sadia and Perdigão are strong Brazilian consumer brands; F1 fit mainly around the São Paulo Grand Prix and Middle East exports.
changed: Formed in 2025 by the merger of Marfrig and BRF

name: Molson Coors Beverage Company
desc: Brews and sells beers such as Coors Light, Miller Lite, Molson Canadian, Blue Moon, Carling and Staropramen.
markets: Main markets the United States, Canada, the UK and Central and Eastern Europe.
rationale: Major sports sponsor in North America and Europe; F1's US races offer reach, though Heineken holds F1's global beer rights.

name: General Mills
desc: Makes packaged foods such as Cheerios, Nature Valley, Pillsbury, Häagen-Dazs and Blue Buffalo pet food for retailers and foodservice.
markets: Sells in more than 100 countries, with the United States the largest market.
rationale: Large consumer advertiser, mostly US-focused; F1 fit is plausible for snack brands but not an obvious strategic match.
changed: Sold its US yogurt business in 2025

name: Domino's Pizza
desc: Pizza delivery and carry-out chain operating mostly franchised stores, with strong digital ordering, in more than 90 countries.
markets: Stores in more than 90 countries; master franchisees run most international markets.
rationale: Highly visible delivery brand with sports marketing; F1 race-weekend promotions could work, but motorsport fit is moderate.

name: Coca-Cola FEMSA
desc: Largest Coca-Cola franchise bottler, producing and distributing soft drinks, water, juices and dairy drinks to retailers.
markets: Operates in Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Guatemala and other Latin American countries.
rationale: Bottler of brands owned by The Coca-Cola Company; F1 decisions sit with the brand owner, so direct fit is weak.

name: Luckin Coffee
desc: Coffee chain selling coffee, tea and snacks through app-based ordering at tens of thousands of stores, mostly in China.
markets: Mainly mainland China, with stores in Singapore, Malaysia and the United States.
rationale: Large young Chinese consumer base and international expansion; F1 and the Chinese Grand Prix could support brand building abroad.
changed: Delisted from Nasdaq in 2020 after an accounting fraud; shares now trade over the counter

name: Tesco
desc: Operates supermarkets, convenience stores and online grocery, plus Booker wholesale, mainly in the UK and Ireland.
markets: Stores in the UK, Ireland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary.
rationale: Dominant UK grocer; British Grand Prix promotions could work, but its domestic focus limits F1's international value.
changed: Sold its retail banking business to Barclays in 2024

name: Starbucks
desc: Coffeehouse chain selling coffee, tea, food and packaged goods through company-operated and licensed stores worldwide.
markets: Stores in over 80 countries, with the United States and China the largest markets.
rationale: Global consumer brand with loyalty programme; F1 fan engagement in the US, Middle East and Asia could fit.
changed: Agreed in 2025 to sell majority control of its China retail business to Boyu Capital

name: Campari Group
desc: Produces and sells spirits and aperitifs, including Aperol, Campari, Wild Turkey, SKYY, Grand Marnier and Appleton Estate.
markets: Sells in about 190 countries, with main markets in the US, Italy and other European countries.
rationale: Premium spirits brands suit F1 hospitality and lifestyle activations; rival spirits groups already partner F1 teams.

name: Ahold Delhaize
desc: Operates supermarket chains including Albert Heijn, Delhaize, Food Lion, Stop & Shop and Giant, plus online grocery.
markets: Stores in the United States and several European countries, including the Netherlands, Belgium and Central Europe.
rationale: Local grocery banners rather than one global brand; F1 fit would be limited to regional promotions.

name: Chipotle Mexican Grill
desc: Fast-casual restaurant chain serving made-to-order burritos, bowls and tacos, mainly through company-owned restaurants.
markets: Mainly United States, with restaurants in Canada and Western Europe and partner-led expansion into the Middle East and Asia.
rationale: Strong US consumer brand starting to expand abroad; F1's US races offer reach to young fans.

name: Restaurant Brands International
desc: Franchises Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes and Firehouse Subs restaurants, earning royalties and rent from franchisees.
markets: More than 30,000 restaurants in over 120 countries across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East.
rationale: Global fast-food brands with large marketing funds; Burger King's international reach suits F1 fan promotions, while McDonald's partners appear on the roster.

name: Compass Group
desc: Contract caterer providing food and support services to businesses, schools, hospitals, sports venues and defence sites.
markets: Operates in over 30 countries, with North America the largest market, plus Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: B2B caterer whose Levy unit runs sports-venue hospitality; F1 hospitality and client entertainment fit, but consumer brand is weak.

name: Ferrero
desc: Makes chocolate and confectionery such as Nutella, Kinder, Ferrero Rocher and Tic Tac, plus biscuits and cereals.
markets: Sells in about 170 countries across Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East.
rationale: Family-owned global confectionery brands; rival Nestlé's KitKat partners F1, showing the category's fit with race audiences.
changed: Acquired WK Kellogg Co in 2025

name: Marfrig (now MBRF Global Foods)
desc: Brazilian meat processor producing beef and processed foods, now operating with BRF as MBRF Global Foods.
markets: Operations in South America and the United States, with exports to more than 100 countries.
rationale: Mainly a B2B beef supplier; consumer F1 value sits with MBRF's Sadia and Perdigão brands rather than Marfrig.
changed: Merged with BRF in 2025 and renamed MBRF Global Foods

name: Elior Group
desc: Contract caterer and services company providing meals and facility services to businesses, schools, hospitals and care homes.
markets: Operates mainly in France, the UK, Spain, Italy and the United States.
rationale: B2B caterer with low consumer recognition; F1 hospitality could help client entertainment, but overall fit is weak.
changed: Merged with Derichebourg Multiservices in 2023, with Derichebourg becoming its largest shareholder

name: Swire Pacific
desc: Hong Kong conglomerate with businesses in property, aviation, Coca-Cola bottling and trading and industrial activities.
markets: Mainly Hong Kong and mainland China, with Coca-Cola bottling in South-East Asia and the western United States.
rationale: Cathay Pacific stake and Coca-Cola bottling give consumer reach; F1 fit is moderate, mostly through hospitality in Asia.

name: Woolworths Group
desc: Operates Woolworths supermarkets, Big W discount stores and Petstock, plus online grocery, in Australia and New Zealand.
markets: Customers in Australia and New Zealand only; no verified wider expansion plans.
rationale: Dominant Australian grocer; Australian Grand Prix promotions could work, but domestic focus limits F1 value.

name: Brinker International
desc: Owns, operates and franchises Chili's Grill & Bar and Maggiano's Little Italy casual dining restaurants.
markets: Mainly United States, with franchised Chili's restaurants in about 30 countries.
rationale: US-focused casual dining brand; F1's American races offer reach, but the international fit is limited.

name: Lamb Weston
desc: Produces frozen potato products such as french fries for quick-service restaurants, foodservice distributors and retailers.
markets: Sells in more than 100 countries, with plants in North America, Europe, China and Australia.
rationale: B2B food supplier with little consumer brand marketing; weak F1 fit beyond customer hospitality.

name: Coca-Cola İçecek
desc: Coca-Cola bottler producing and distributing sparkling drinks, juices, water and tea in Turkey, Pakistan and Central Asia.
markets: Operates in Turkey, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Jordan, Bangladesh and other Central Asian countries.
rationale: Bottler of brands owned by The Coca-Cola Company; sponsorship decisions sit with the brand owner, so F1 fit is weak.

name: Mixue Group
desc: Mostly franchised chain selling low-priced ice cream, tea drinks and coffee, supplying franchisees with ingredients and equipment.
markets: Mainly mainland China, with stores in South-East Asia and other Asian markets.
rationale: Huge budget consumer brand in China and South-East Asia; low-price positioning gives limited fit with F1's premium image.
changed: Listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in 2025

name: Minerva Foods
desc: Slaughters cattle and sells beef, lamb and by-products to retailers, foodservice companies and importers.
markets: Plants in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Colombia and Australia, exporting to more than 100 countries.
rationale: Mainly a B2B commodity exporter with limited consumer branding; weak F1 fit.

name: Olam Group
desc: Agri-business supplying cocoa, coffee, nuts, spices, grains and other food ingredients to food manufacturers and traders.
markets: Sources and sells in dozens of countries across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas.
rationale: B2B ingredients supplier with little consumer brand; weak F1 fit beyond client hospitality.
changed: Reorganised into ofi, Olam Agri and remaining businesses from 2020

name: Gruma
desc: Produces corn flour and tortillas under brands such as Mission, Maseca and Guerrero for retailers and foodservice.
markets: Main markets the United States and Mexico, with plants in Central America, Europe, Asia and Oceania.
rationale: Mission and Maseca brands reach US and Mexican consumers; F1 fit around Mexico City and US races is plausible.

name: Haidilao International Holding
desc: Operates Haidilao hot pot restaurants known for table-side service, mainly in mainland China.
markets: Restaurants mainly in mainland China; overseas restaurants were spun off into Super Hi International.
rationale: Strong Chinese consumer brand; Chinese Grand Prix promotions could work, but its domestic focus limits F1 value.
changed: Spun off its overseas restaurants as Super Hi International in 2022

name: Coca-Cola HBC
desc: Coca-Cola bottler producing and distributing soft drinks, water, energy drinks and coffee in Europe and Africa.
markets: Operates in about 29 countries across Western, Central and Eastern Europe, Nigeria and Egypt.
rationale: Bottler of brands owned by The Coca-Cola Company and Monster; F1 sponsorship decisions sit with brand owners, so fit is weak.
changed: Agreed in 2025 to buy a majority stake in Coca-Cola Beverages Africa

name: Kimberly-Clark
desc: Makes personal care and tissue products such as Huggies, Kleenex, Cottonelle, Scott and Kotex for consumers and businesses.
markets: Sells in about 175 countries across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
rationale: Large household-brand advertiser; F1 fit is moderate, mostly for consumer promotions rather than a natural brand link.
changed: Agreed in November 2025 to acquire Kenvue

name: Wayfair
desc: Online retailer of furniture, decor and housewares under Wayfair, AllModern, Birch Lane and Perigold, now opening physical stores.
markets: Customers in the United States, Canada and the UK; exited Germany in 2024.
rationale: Heavy consumer marketer focused on North America; F1's US fan growth offers reach, though motorsport fit is limited.

name: Haleon
desc: Consumer health company selling Sensodyne, Advil, Panadol, Voltaren, Centrum and other over-the-counter and oral health products.
markets: Sells in more than 100 markets across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
rationale: Global consumer health brands could use F1 for wellness and performance messaging, but the motorsport link is indirect.
changed: Spun off from GSK in 2022

name: Seagate Technology
desc: Makes hard disk drives, solid-state drives and storage systems for data centres, cloud providers, PCs and consumers.
markets: Sells worldwide to cloud and enterprise customers in North America, Asia-Pacific and Europe.
rationale: Data storage is central to F1 telemetry and AI; a technology partnership could showcase products to enterprise customers.

name: Amer Sports
desc: Sporting goods group selling Arc'teryx, Salomon, Wilson and Atomic apparel, footwear and equipment through retail and wholesale.
markets: Sells worldwide, with large businesses in the Americas, Europe and Greater China.
rationale: Premium sports brands with strong Chinese growth; F1 lifestyle collaborations could fit Arc'teryx or Salomon.
changed: Acquired by an Anta Sports-led consortium in 2019 and listed on the NYSE in 2024

name: Lazada
desc: E-commerce marketplace connecting brands and sellers with consumers, with logistics and payments services, in South-East Asia.
markets: Operates in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
rationale: Large South-East Asian consumer platform; Singapore Grand Prix promotions could fit, mostly regional marketing value.
changed: Majority-acquired by Alibaba in 2016

name: Newell Brands
desc: Makes consumer products such as Rubbermaid, Sharpie, Paper Mate, Graco, Coleman, Yankee Candle and Oster.
markets: Main market the United States, with sales in many countries across the Americas, Europe and Asia.
rationale: Portfolio of household brands with no single flagship; F1 fit is weak beyond retail promotions.
changed: Renamed from Newell Rubbermaid after acquiring Jarden in 2016

name: Hanesbrands
desc: Makes innerwear and basic apparel under Hanes, Bonds, Maidenform, Playtex and Bali, sold through retailers and online.
markets: Main markets the United States and Australia, with sales in other countries in the Americas and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Mass basics brands now inside Gildan; weak F1 fit beyond merchandise supply.
changed: Acquired by Gildan Activewear in 2025

name: Rappi
desc: Delivery app offering restaurant meals, groceries and pharmacy products, plus RappiPay financial services and Rappi Prime subscriptions.
markets: Operates in Latin America, including Colombia, Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru and Costa Rica.
rationale: Strong Latin American consumer brand; Mexico City and São Paulo Grands Prix offer regional promotions.

name: Trade Republic
desc: Online broker and bank letting retail customers buy stocks, ETFs and crypto, run savings plans and use cards.
markets: Millions of retail customers across Germany, France, Italy, Spain and other European countries.
rationale: Fast-growing consumer brand in Europe; trading and fintech rivals such as eToro and Revolut already sponsor F1.

name: Essity
desc: Makes hygiene and health products such as Tork, TENA, Libero, Libresse, Bodyform and Leukoplast for consumers and institutions.
markets: Sells in about 150 countries, with main markets in Europe, North America, Latin America and Asia.
rationale: Hygiene brands with limited motorsport link; Tork could suit B2B venue hygiene, but overall F1 fit is modest.
changed: Spun off from SCA in 2017

name: Whatnot
desc: Live-stream shopping marketplace where sellers auction trading cards, collectibles, sneakers and fashion to buyers via its app.
markets: Operates in the United States, Canada, the UK and several European countries.
rationale: Collector audience overlaps with F1 trading cards and memorabilia; live auctions of racing collectibles could fit.

name: Walmart
desc: World's largest retailer, operating supercenters, discount stores, Sam's Club warehouses and e-commerce, plus Flipkart in India.
markets: Mainly United States, plus Mexico, Central America, Canada, Chile, China, India and South Africa.
rationale: Huge US advertiser; F1's American growth could support retail promotions and retail media, though fit is moderate.
changed: Moved its stock listing from the NYSE to Nasdaq in 2025

name: Primo Brands
desc: Sells bottled water brands such as Poland Spring, Deer Park and Arrowhead, plus home and office water delivery.
markets: Customers in the United States and Canada; no verified wider expansion plans.
rationale: US-focused water brands; F1 hydration messaging at US races is plausible, but international reach is lacking.
changed: Formed in 2024 by the merger of Primo Water and BlueTriton Brands
